title: Comparing decimals with ==
summary: Why comparing decimal numbers with == can give a surprising false result, and how to check whether values are close enough instead.
objectives: Explain why some decimal values are stored as nearby approximations in Java.
Trace a decimal comparison and predict whether `==` is true or false.
Tell the difference between a compile-time error and a result that is wrong at run time.
Use a tolerance to check whether two calculated decimal values are close enough.

blocks.text: The `==` operator asks whether two values are exactly equal. That is often fine for whole numbers. With decimal values stored as `double`, it can be a trap. Some decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly, so a calculation may produce a nearby value instead.

bad.title: Looks equal, but prints false

good.title: Check whether the values are close

blocks.note: Both programs compile. The first comparison runs and prints `false`; this is a run-time result, not a compile-time error. The second checks whether the difference is smaller than a chosen tolerance, meaning an allowed amount of difference.

blocks.text: A `double` stores a binary floating-point value. Binary means a number system based on 2. Some decimal fractions, such as `0.1`, do not have an exact finite form in that system. Java stores the nearest available value. Calculations use those stored values, so the result may be slightly different from the decimal value you expected.

blocks.caption: How nearby stored values can make an exact comparison false

flowchart TD

  B --> C[Calculate using stored values]
  C --> D{Are the stored results exactly equal?}
  D -- yes --> E[Print true]
  D -- no --> F[Print false]

blocks.title: A tolerance is a choice
blocks.text: The tolerance in the example is much larger than the tiny difference, so the check prints `true`. Choose a tolerance that makes sense for the precision your program needs. It is not one universal number.

Trace each step in order. The exact stored values are not the same as the simple decimal spellings shown in the code. The important point is that the calculation and the `0.3` value do not end up exactly equal.

blocks.caption: Tracing `double total = 0.1 + 0.2;` followed by `total == 0.3`
rows: Stores the literal `0.3` as a `double` value
This is a nearby value too
`false`, because the stored values are not exactly equal

blocks.text: The comparison in the last row does not estimate whether the values look close. It asks whether they are exactly equal. That is why the first program prints `false` without any compiler warning.
In each example, first predict what exact equality will do. Then compare that result with a tolerance check.

bad.title: Adding two decimal values

good.title: Check the difference from the target

blocks.note: `Math.abs` gives the absolute value, which removes the negative sign if there is one. The program checks whether the difference is less than `0.000001`.

bad.title: A decimal average compared exactly

good.title: Compare the average with a tolerance

blocks.note: The average calculation can also produce a nearby value rather than exactly `0.2`. The tolerance check accepts a small difference.

blocks.text: The problem is not limited to adding two values. Any calculation with decimal values can lead to an exact comparison that surprises you.

bad.title: Subtracting decimal values, then using exact equality

good.title: Check whether the difference is small

blocks.note: The comparison in the first version may be `false` because of the stored approximations. The second version asks whether the values are close enough.

bad.title: Assuming a calculated amount equals a decimal literal

good.title: Use a tolerance for the calculated amount

blocks.note: Multiplication can also produce a nearby result. The safe reasoning is the same: if a small difference is acceptable, check the size of that difference.

blocks.title: When exact equality is useful
blocks.text: For whole-number values such as `int` values, `==` checks whether the values are equal. For calculated `double` values, first ask whether you need exact equality or whether a small difference is acceptable.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The code compiles. At run time, `==` checks exact equality, and the calculated value is not exactly the same as the stored value for `0.3`.

blocks.question: Which condition checks whether `value` is within `0.000001` of `target`?
blocks.explanation: `Math.abs(value - target)` measures the size of the difference without a negative sign. The condition is true when that difference is less than the tolerance.

blocks.question: Is `double answer = 0.1 + 0.2; System.out.println(answer == 0.3);` a compile-time error or a run-time result?
options: A compiler warning that stops the program
blocks.explanation: Java allows this code to compile. When it runs, the exact comparison evaluates to `false` and that value is printed.

items: `==` asks whether two values are exactly equal.
Some decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly as `double` values, so calculations can produce nearby results.
A decimal comparison with `==` can compile normally and still print a surprising result at run time.
When a small difference is acceptable, compare `Math.abs(value - target)` with a suitable tolerance.
Choose the tolerance based on how much difference your program can accept.
